Apply lemma_110 with Q in place of q to this projective bundle (with a rank-c vector bundle N on Z such that E = P(N) in the convention of lemma_110; if the normal bundle convention gives the dual, the formula is identical). The lemma does not require Z to be connected, so it applies to the possibly disconnected Z. For n=d it gives an F-equivariant isomorphism Phi: direct sum_{j=0}^{c-1} H^{d-2j}(Z) -> H^d(E), (x_j) -> sum_j p^*x_j cup xi^j, where xi = c_1(O_E(1)) and F_E corresponds to Q^j F_Z on the j-th summand. The j=0 summand maps isomorphically onto p^*H^d(Z). Therefore Phi induces an F-equivariant isomorphism Phi_+: direct sum_{j=1}^{c-1} H^{d-2j}(Z) -> H^d(E)/p^*H^d(Z), with F_E acting on the j-th summand as Q^j F_Z. For c=1 both sides are zero: the sum is empty and H^d(E) = p^*H^d(Z). Terms with d-2j<0 are zero by convention.

Step 5 (final decomposition). Combining Theta, Psi, and Phi_+, define Xi: H^d(Xtilde) -> H^d(X) direct sum direct sum_{i=1}^{c-1} H^{d-2i}(Z) by Xi(w) = (s(w), Phi_+^{-1}(Psi([w]))). Each ingredient is a Q_l-linear isomorphism and F-equivariant, so Xi is a Q_l-linear isomorphism. For w in H^d(Xtilde), Xi(F_Xtilde w) = (s(F_Xtilde w), Phi_+^{-1}(Psi([F_Xtilde w]))) = (F_X s(w), Phi_+^{-1}(F_E Psi([w]))) = (F_X s(w), (Q^i F_Z)_{i=1}^{c-1} Phi_+^{-1}(Psi([w]))). Thus under Xi the operator F_Xtilde corresponds to F_X on H^d(X) and to Q^i F_Z on the i-th summand H^{d-2i}(Z), for i=1,...,c-1. Since Q=q^m, this is exactly the required Frobenius compatibility. The case Z empty was handled in Step 0; the case c=1 is included as the empty sum and zero quotient. This completes the proof."
}

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(Z\subset\mathbb P^2_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\) be a closed subscheme that is finite etale over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and let \(S=\operatorname{Bl}_Z\mathbb P^2_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\) be the blow-up of \(\mathbb P^2_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\) along \(Z\). Then the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}_{S_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\), is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every integer \(n\ge0\), and its scalar extension to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is diagonalizable.
proof:
Proof. Put Q=q^m and k=bar F_q. All Frobenius operators in this proof are the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius F=(id×Spec σ)^*, σ(c)=c^Q; this is exactly the operator in the statement because Q=q^m. We first record two cohomological computations.

(1) Projective plane. Apply lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_201 with its q replaced by Q and with n=2. It gives an isomorphism of graded Q_l[F]-algebras Q_l[t]/(t^3) → ⊕_{r≥0} H^r_et(P^2_k,Q_l), t^i↦h^i, where h=c_1(O(1)), and F(t^i)=Q^i t^i for 0≤i≤2. Hence H^r_et(P^2_k,Q_l)=0 unless r=0,2,4, and on H^{2i}_et(P^2_k,Q_l) the operator F is multiplication by the scalar Q^i. A scalar operator is semisimple, and the zero space is trivially semisimple. Thus F is semisimple on H^r_et(P^2_k,Q_l) for every r≥0.

(2) Finite étale center. Assume first Z is nonempty. Let A=Γ(Z,O_Z). Since Z is finite étale over F_Q, A is a finite étale F_Q-algebra. Because k is algebraically closed, A⊗_{F_Q}k ≅ k^{Z(k)}; equivalently Z_k ≅ ∐_{z∈Z(k)} Spec k. The set Z(k) is finite. By iterating Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_cohom_open_closed_sum, H^r_et(Z_k,Q_l) ≅ ⊕_{z∈Z(k)} H^r_et(Spec k,Q_l) for every r. For Spec k, the global-sections functor on the small étale site is exact: every étale cover of Spec k has a section because k is separably closed, so a short exact sequence of sheaves gives a short exact sequence on global sections. Therefore H^0_et(Spec k,Q_l)=Q_l and H^r_et(Spec k,Q_l)=0 for r>0. Consequently H^0_et(Z_k,Q_l)=⊕_{z∈Z(k)} Q_l e_z, where e_z is the unit of the z-th component, and H^r_et(Z_k,Q_l)=0 for r>0. The map id_Z×Spec σ is an automorphism of Z_k (σ fixes F_Q), so it permutes the components; on H^0 it sends e_z to e_{τ(z)} for some permutation τ of the finite set Z(k). Lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_79, applied with c=1, then shows that F is semisimple on H^0_et(Z_k,Q_l). On H^r_et(Z_k,Q_l)=0 for r>0, F is trivially semisimple. Thus F is semisimple on H^r_et(Z_k,Q_l) for every r≥0.

(3) Blow-up. Assume Z is nonempty. We use lemma eoinm/c9a724f5aa70a2d3/4ca7f1. Its statement is: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let l≠p be a prime, let m≥1, and put k=bar F_q. Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d≥2 over F_{q^m}, let Z⊂X be a smooth closed subvariety of pure codimension 2 defined over F_{q^m}, and let π:X~=Bl_Z X→X be the blow-up. Then for every integer n≥0, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id×Spec σ)^*, σ(u)=u^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_et(X~_k,Q_l) if and only if it is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) and on H^{n-2}_et(Z_k,Q_l), where H^j_et(Z_k,Q_l)=0 for j<0. We verify its hypotheses. Take X=P^2_{F_Q}. Then X is smooth, projective and geometrically connected of pure dimension d=2≥2. The nonempty scheme Z is finite étale over F_Q, hence reduced and smooth over F_Q of relative dimension 0; as a closed subscheme of X it is of pure dimension 0, and since X is pure of dimension 2 it is of pure codimension 2 in X. It is defined over F_Q by hypothesis. The morphism π:S=Bl_Z X→X is the blow-up in the statement. The Frobenius convention is exactly the Q=q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, with no Tate twist. Therefore, for every n≥0, F is semisimple on H^n_et(S_k,Q_l) if and only if F is semisimple on H^n_et(P^2_k,Q_l) and on H^{n-2}_et(Z_k,Q_l) (the latter group being 0 for n<2). By (1) and (2), both conditions hold for every n. Hence F is semisimple on H^n_et(S_k,Q_l) for every n≥0.

(4) Empty center. If Z=∅, then the blow-up of P^2 along the empty subscheme is P^2 itself (the ideal sheaf is O_{P^2}). Thus S≅P^2_{F_Q}, and (1) again gives semisimplicity of F on H^n_et(S_k,Q_l) for every n≥0.

(5) Diagonalizability. In both the empty and nonempty cases, S is proper over F_Q: it is either P^2 or the blow-up of the proper scheme P^2 along a closed subscheme, and blow-ups of proper schemes are proper. Apply lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob with its q replaced by Q, with X=S, and with K=Q_l equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism. It follows that H^n_et(S_k,Q_l) is finite-dimensional over Q_l for every n≥0. Now fix n. By (3) or (4), F is semisimple on the finite-dimensional Q_l-vector space V=H^n_et(S_k,Q_l). Lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5, applied to V and T=F, says that F is semisimple on V if and only if F⊗id is diagonalizable on V⊗_{Q_l} bar Q_l. Therefore the scalar extension of F to bar Q_l is diagonalizable on H^n_et(S_k,Q_l)⊗_{Q_l} bar Q_l. This holds for every n≥0, completing the proof.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_q\). Suppose that the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_m)^*\), \(\sigma_m(c)=c^{q^m}\), is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every integer \(n\ge0\). Then the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every integer \(n\ge0\).
proof:
The assertion is precisely the direction "$F_{q^m}$ semisimple $\Rightarrow$ $F_q$ semisimple" of the equivalence recorded in eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_150. We first record that citation, then spell out the argument in full so that no step is left implicit.

Step 0 (matching of hypotheses). In the notation of eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_150, take the given prime power $q=p^a$, the given prime $\ell\neq p$, the given $m\ge 1$, the variety $X$ (which is smooth and projective over $\mathbb F_q$, hence in particular a smooth projective variety over $\mathbb F_q$ in the sense of that lemma; the additional hypothesis of geometric connectedness is not needed), $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, and an arbitrary integer $n\ge 0$. For $s\ge1$ let $\sigma_s:k\to k$, $c\mapsto c^{q^s}$, and let $F_{q^s}:=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_s)^*$ and $G_{q^s}:=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_s^{-1})^*$ be the induced $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphisms of $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. With these choices eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_150 states exactly that $F_q$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ if and only if $F_{q^m}$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Since $F_{q^m}$ is semisimple by the hypothesis of the lemma under proof, $F_q$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. As $n\ge0$ was arbitrary, the conclusion follows. This already completes the proof.

For completeness, and to make the dependence transparent, here is the elementary derivation of the same implication, which is the content of the direction just used.

Step 1 (finite-dimensionality). Fix $n\ge0$ and put $V:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Since $X$ is projective, it is proper over $\mathbb F_q$. Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob to the proper $\mathbb F_q$-variety $X$, to $K=\mathbb Q_\ell\in D^b_c(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ (the constant sheaf, equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism $\psi:F_X^*\mathbb Q_\ell\to\mathbb Q_\ell$) and to the integer $n$, we obtain that $V$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$.

Step 2 (invertibility). By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a (applied to the scheme $X$ over $\mathbb F_q$, the algebraic closure $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, the $q$-power automorphism $\sigma=\sigma_1$ of $k$, the prime $\ell\neq p$ and $i=n$), the pullback $F_1:=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_1)^*$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $V$; in particular it is an invertible $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear operator on the finite-dimensional space $V$.

Step 3 (the identity $F_{q^m}=F_q^{\,m}$). First, $\sigma_m=\sigma_1^m$ as endomorphisms of $k$: for every $c\in k$ one has $\sigma_1^m(c)=c^{q^m}=\sigma_m(c)$. Applying the functor $\operatorname{Spec}$ gives $\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_m=(\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_1)^m$ as endomorphisms of $\operatorname{Spec}k$. Each $\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_s$ is a morphism of $\mathbb F_q$-schemes, because $\sigma_s$ fixes $\mathbb F_q$ pointwise: for $c\in\mathbb F_q$ one has $c^{q}=c$ (the elements of $\mathbb F_q$ are exactly the roots of $T^q-T$), hence $c^{q^s}=c$ for all $s\ge1$. Now $X_k=X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k$, and the endomorphism $\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_s$ is the image of $\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_s$ under the base-change functor $Y\mapsto Y_k=Y\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k$ from $\mathbb F_q$-schemes to $k$-schemes. A functor preserves composition, so
\[
\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_m
=\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times(\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_1)^m
=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_1)^m
\]
as endomorphisms of $X_k$. Étale cohomology with $\mathbb Q_\ell$-coefficients is a contravariant functor on $k$-schemes, so pullback reverses composition; applying it to the displayed identity yields
\[
F_{q^m}=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_m)^*
=\bigl((\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_1)^m\bigr)^*
=\bigl((\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_1)^*\bigr)^m
=F_q^{\,m}
\]
as $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear endomorphisms of $V$.

Step 4 (removing the $m$-th power). By hypothesis, $F_{q^m}$ is semisimple on $V$; by Step 3 this says that $F_q^{\,m}$ is semisimple on $V$. The space $V$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ (Step 1) and $F_q$ is an invertible $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear operator on $V$ (Step 2), and $m\ge1$. Hence eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_35(iii) (with $T=F_q$ and exponent $m$) gives that $F_q$ itself is semisimple on $V=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

Step 5 (conclusion). The integer $n\ge0$ was arbitrary in Steps 1–4, so the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius $(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every integer $n\ge0$, as claimed. Note that the case $m=1$ is the tautological case (hypothesis and conclusion coincide), and it is also covered by the argument above since then $F_{q^m}=F_q$.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(M\ge1\), let \(C_1,\dots,C_M\) be smooth projective geometrically connected curves over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and suppose that there exists a proper surjective generically finite morphism \(C_1\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}C_M\to X\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Then the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\), is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every integer \(n\ge0\).
proof:
**Notation.** Put \(F=\mathbb F_{q^m}\) and \(q'=q^m=p^{am}\), so that \(q'\) is a prime power with \(F=\mathbb F_{q'}\). Put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q'}\). Let
\[
P=C_1\times_{F}C_2\times_F\cdots\times_F C_M
\]\nbe the fibre product over \(F\), and let \(f:P\to X\) be the given proper surjective generically finite morphism over \(F\). For a scheme \(Z\) over \(F\) and an integer \(n\ge0\) write
\[
F_Z:=(\operatorname{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\in\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\bigl(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr),\qquad \sigma(c)=c^{q'}=c^{q^m},
\]\nfor the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius; this is an automorphism by [eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a] applied with \(q'\) in place of \(q\). We must show that \(F_X\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\). (The argument does not use the value of \(d\); only the surjectivity of \(f\) will be used, not its generic finiteness.)

**Step 1: \(P\) is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(F\).**

Each \(C_i\) is, by hypothesis, a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \(F\), i.e. a smooth projective \(F\)-scheme of pure relative dimension \(1\) whose base change to \(k\) is connected.

*(a) Projectivity.* Choose closed immersions \(C_i\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^{n_i}_F\). The product of closed immersions is a closed immersion \(P\hookrightarrow\prod_{i=1}^M\mathbb P^{n_i}_F\), and the Segre embedding \(\prod_{i=1}^M\mathbb P^{n_i}_F\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_F\) (with \(N=\prod_i(n_i+1)-1\)) is a closed immersion. A composition of closed immersions is a closed immersion, so \(P\) is projective over \(F\), hence proper over \(F\).

*(b) Smoothness and pure dimension \(M\).* The structure morphism \(P\to\operatorname{Spec}F\) factors as the composition of the \(M\) projection morphisms \(P\to C_1\times_F\cdots\widehat{C_i}\cdots\times_FC_M\); the \(i\)-th such projection is the base change of the smooth morphism \(C_i\to\operatorname{Spec}F\) of relative dimension \(1\), hence is smooth of relative dimension \(1\). A composition of smooth morphisms is smooth and relative dimensions add, so \(P\to\operatorname{Spec}F\) is smooth of relative dimension \(M\). In particular \(P\) is a smooth \(F\)-variety of pure dimension \(M\).

*(c) Geometric connectedness.* Since \(C_i\) is geometrically connected, \((C_i)_k=C_i\times_F k\) is a nonempty connected \(k\)-scheme of finite type, and \(P_k=\prod_{i=1}^M (C_i)_k\). We use the standard fact that a fibre product over an algebraically closed field of two nonempty connected \(k\)-schemes of finite type is connected. Indeed, for such \(A,B\), suppose \(A\times_kB=U\sqcup V\) with \(U,V\) nonempty open and closed. For each \(b\in B\) the fibre \(A\times\{b\}\cong A\) is connected, hence lies entirely in \(U\) or entirely in \(V\); set \(B_U=\{b: A\times\{b\}\subseteq U\}\) and \(B_V=\{b: A\times\{b\}\subseteq V\}\). These are disjoint and cover \(B\), and both are nonempty because the projection \(A\times_kB\to B\) is surjective and \(U,V\neq\varnothing\). That projection is flat (base change of \(A\to\operatorname{Spec}k\), and any scheme over a field is flat) and locally of finite presentation, hence open, so \(B_U\) and \(B_V\) are open; this contradicts the connectedness of \(B\). Iterating this argument over the \(M\) factors shows that \(P_k\) is connected, i.e. \(P\) is geometrically connected over \(F\).

**Step 2: \(F_P\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).**

Apply [eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_341] with the prime power \(q'\) in place of its \(q\), with \(M\) in place of its \(m\), and with the curves \(C_1,\dots,C_M\) over \(\mathbb F_{q'}=F\). All hypotheses hold: \(q'=p^{am}\) is a prime power, \(M\ge1\), each \(C_i\) is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \(\mathbb F_{q'}\), \(\overline{\mathbb F}_{q'}=k\), and \(\ell\neq p\). The lemma gives that the \(q'\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}_{P_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q'}\), acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every integer \(n\ge0\). By definition this operator is \(F_P\).

**Step 3: \(f^*\) is injective and Frobenius-equivariant.**

By [eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_375] applied over the field \(\mathbb F_{q'}=F\) (with \(q'\) in place of its \(q\), with \(Y=P\) and \(X=X\)), for every \(n\ge0\) the pullback
\[\nf^*=f_k^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)
\]\nis injective: \(f\) is a surjective morphism of smooth projective geometrically connected varieties over \(\mathbb F_{q'}\) by Step 1 and the hypotheses, and \(\ell\neq p\).

By [eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_214] applied over \(\mathbb F_{q'}\) to the morphism \(f:P\to X\), for every \(n\ge0\) we have
\[\nf^*\circ F_X=F_P\circ f^*.
\]
Hence, for each \(n\ge0\), the subspace
\[
W_n:=\operatorname{im}\bigl(f^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)
\]\nis \(F_P\)-stable; more precisely \(F_P(W_n)=\operatorname{im}(F_P\circ f^*)=\operatorname{im}(f^*\circ F_X)=f^*(H^n(X_k))=W_n\), using that \(F_X\) is surjective (it is an automorphism). Since \(f^*\) is injective, it induces a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism
\[
\alpha_n:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }W_n,\qquad \alpha_n\circ F_X=(F_P|_{W_n})\circ\alpha_n .
\]

**Step 4: Finite-dimensionality.**

Apply [eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob] over \(\mathbb F_{q'}\) (with \(q'\) in place of its \(q\)) to the proper \(\mathbb F_{q'}\)-variety \(P\) and to the constant sheaf \(K=\mathbb Q_\ell\) on \(P_k\) equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism \(\psi:F_P^*\mathbb Q_\ell\to\mathbb Q_\ell\). It yields that \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) for every \(n\). The same lemma applied to the proper \(\mathbb F_{q'}\)-variety \(X\) yields that \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is finite-dimensional for every \(n\). Consequently \(W_n\subseteq H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is finite-dimensional as well.

**Step 5: Conclusion.**

Fix \(n\ge0\). By Step 2, \(F_P\) is a semisimple \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear operator on the finite-dimensional space \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), and it is invertible by [eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a]. Since \(W_n\) is an \(F_P\)-stable \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear subspace, [eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_515] shows that the restriction \(F_P|_{W_n}\) is semisimple on \(W_n\). The isomorphism \(\alpha_n:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to W_n\) satisfies \(\alpha_n\circ F_X=(F_P|_{W_n})\circ\alpha_n\), both operators \(F_X\) and \(F_P|_{W_n}\) are invertible (for \(F_X\) use [eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a]; for \(F_P|_{W_n}\) use \(F_P(W_n)=W_n\) and invertibility of \(F_P\)), and both spaces are finite-dimensional by Step 4. Hence [eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8] gives that \(F_X\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).

As \(n\ge0\) was arbitrary, the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\), is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every integer \(n\ge0\), as required.

statement: Let \(M\ge1\), let \(G_1,\dots,G_M\) be groups, and let \(H\) be a subgroup of finite index in \(G_1\times\cdots\times G_M\). Then there exist subgroups \(K_i\le G_i\) of finite index such that \(K_1\times\cdots\times K_M\subseteq H\).
proof:
Let \(G=G_1\times\cdots\times G_M\), and for each \(i\) let \(\pi_i:G\to G_i\) be the \(i\)-th projection. Put \(n=[G:H]\), which is finite by hypothesis; if \(n=1\) then \(H=G\) and the choice \(K_i=G_i\) works, so we may assume \(n\ge 1\) in the argument below (the argument in fact covers \(n=1\) as well).

**Step 1 (the kernel of the action on cosets).** Consider the left action of \(G\) on the finite set \(G/H\) of left cosets, given by \(g\cdot(xH)=gxH\). It corresponds to a group homomorphism
\[
\rho:G\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sym}(G/H),
\]
where \(\operatorname{Sym}(G/H)\) is the symmetric group on the \(n\)-element set \(G/H\), hence has order \(n!\). Let
\[
N=\ker\rho=\{\,g\in G : gxH=xH \text{ for all } x\in G\,\}.
\]
Since \(N\) is a kernel of a homomorphism, it is a normal subgroup of \(G\). Since \(G/N\) embeds into the finite group \(\operatorname{Sym}(G/H)\) via \(\rho\), we have
\[
[G:N]=\#(G/N)\le n!<\infty,
\]
so \(N\) has finite index in \(G\).

**Step 2 (identification of \(N\) and \(N\subseteq H\)).** For \(g,x\in G\) we have \(gxH=xH\) if and only if \(x^{-1}gx\in H\). Hence
\[
N=\{\,g\in G : x^{-1}gx\in H \text{ for all } x\in G\,\}=\bigcap_{x\in G} xHx^{-1}.
\]
In particular, taking \(x=e\) (the identity of \(G\)) gives the term \(H\) in the intersection, so
\[
N\subseteq H.
\]

**Step 3 (the subgroups \(K_i\)).** Identify \(G_i\) with the subgroup \(\{1\}\times\cdots\times G_i\times\cdots\times\{1\}\) of \(G\), and define
\[
K_i := N\cap G_i \;=\; G_i\cap N .
\]
Being an intersection of subgroups, \(K_i\) is a subgroup of \(G_i\). (Concretely, \(K_i=\{\,g\in G_i : g\in N\,\}\), the tuples whose only possibly nontrivial entry is in the \(i\)-th position and which lie in \(N\).)

**Step 4 (\(K_i\) has finite index in \(G_i\)).** Let \(\varphi_i:G_i\hookrightarrow G\twoheadrightarrow G/N\) be the composite of the inclusion \(G_i\subseteq G\) with the quotient map \(G\to G/N\); this is a group homomorphism. Its kernel is
\[
\ker\varphi_i=\{\,g\in G_i : g\in N\,\}=G_i\cap N=K_i .
\]
Hence \(\varphi_i\) induces an injective homomorphism \(G_i/K_i\hookrightarrow G/N\). Since \(G/N\) is finite (Step 1), the group \(G_i/K_i\) is finite, i.e.
\[
[G_i:K_i]=\#(G_i/K_i)\le \#(G/N)<\infty .
\]
Thus each \(K_i\) is a subgroup of \(G_i\) of finite index, as required.

**Step 5 (\(K_1\times\cdots\times K_M\subseteq H\)).** Let \(k_i\in K_i\) for \(i=1,\dots,M\). Viewing \(k_i\) as the element of \(G\) with \(i\)-th coordinate \(k_i\) and all other coordinates \(1\), we have \(k_i\in N\) by definition of \(K_i=N\cap G_i\). Since \(N\) is a subgroup of \(G\), it is closed under multiplication, so
\[
k_1k_2\cdots k_M\in N .
\]
Under the identification \(G=G_1\times\cdots\times G_M\), the product \(k_1k_2\cdots k_M\) is exactly the tuple \((k_1,\dots,k_M)\). Hence every element of the subgroup
\[
K_1\times\cdots\times K_M=\{\,(k_1,\dots,k_M) : k_i\in K_i\,\}
\]
lies in \(N\). Therefore
\[
K_1\times\cdots\times K_M\subseteq N\subseteq H,
\]
the second inclusion being Step 2.

**Conclusion.** We have produced subgroups \(K_i\le G_i\) with \([G_i:K_i]<\infty\) for all \(i\) and \(K_1\times\cdots\times K_M\subseteq H\). This proves the lemma. (Note that no claim is made, and none is true in general, that \(H\) itself is a product of subgroups; the argument only produces a product of finite-index subgroups sitting inside \(H\).)

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(d\ge1\), and let \(U=\mathbb A^d_{\mathbb F_q}\setminus\{0\}\). Let \(F\) be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\operatorname{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), acting on compactly supported étale cohomology with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-coefficients, and let \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) be the one-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell[F]\)-module on which \(F\) acts by \(q^d\). Then there is an isomorphism of graded \(\mathbb Q_\ell[F]\)-modules \[H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\cong \mathbb Q_\ell[-1]\oplus\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)[-2d],\] where \(\mathbb Q_\ell[-1]\) denotes a copy of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) placed in degree \(1\) with trivial \(F\)-action and \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)[-2d]\) denotes a copy of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) placed in degree \(2d\).
proof:
Let k be an algebraic closure of F_q. Put X = P^d_{F_q}, let H = {x_0=0} ≅ P^{d-1}_{F_q}, let O = [1:0:...:0], and let Y = O ⊔ H. Then Y is a closed subscheme of X defined over F_q and X∖Y = A^d_{F_q}∖{0}. After base change to k we have U_k = X_k∖Y_k. Apply the localization lemma [Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_localization_les_finite_type] to X_k, Y_k, U_k. Since X_k is proper, the groups H^m_{et,c}(U_k,Q_l) occurring there are the usual compactly supported cohomology groups. We obtain a long exact sequence of Q_l-vector spaces
... → C^m → A^m --α_m→ B^m → C^{m+1} → ... ,
where C^m = H^m_{et,c}(U_k,Q_l), A^m = H^m_{et}(X_k,Q_l), B^m = H^m_{et}(Y_k,Q_l), and α_m is restriction to Y_k. The localization triangle j_!Q_l → Q_l → i_*Q_l is functorial, and the arithmetic Frobenius F_X is an automorphism of X_k preserving U_k and Y_k; using the canonical isomorphism F_X^*Q_l ≅ Q_l, the displayed sequence is an exact sequence of Q_l[F]-modules. Thus all maps below are F-equivariant.

By [eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_201], A^m = 0 unless m=2i with 0≤i≤d, and A^{2i} = Q_l h^i, where h = c_1(O_X(1)); moreover F(h^i) = q^i h^i. In particular A^0 = Q_l with trivial F and A^{2d} = Q_l(-d).

Since Y_k = O_k ⊔ H_k, H^m(Y_k,Q_l) = H^m(O_k,Q_l) ⊕ H^m(H_k,Q_l). H^*(O_k) is Q_l in degree 0 with trivial F. For H_k, if d≥2 use [eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_201] for P^{d-1}; if d=1 then H_k = P^0_k and H^*(H_k) is Q_l in degree 0 with trivial F. Hence B^0 = Q_l^2 with trivial F; B^{2i} = Q_l with F = q^i for 1≤i≤d-1; all other B^m are zero.

Let h_H = c_1(O_H(1)). The pullback i_H^*: H^*(X_k) → H^*(H_k) sends h to h_H because i_H^*O_X(1) ≅ O_H(1); hence i_H^*(h^i) = h_H^i. The pullback to O is the identity in degree 0 and zero in positive degrees. Therefore α_0(q) = (q,q); α_{2i} is an isomorphism for 1≤i≤d-1; α_{2d} = 0; all other α_m are zero. These maps commute with F.

For every m≥0, with A^{-1}=B^{-1}=0, exactness gives
0 → B^{m-1}/α_{m-1}(A^{m-1}) → C^m → ker α_m → 0. (1)
Indeed, the kernel of C^m→A^m is the image of B^{m-1}, and the image of C^m in A^m is ker α_m.

From the descriptions:
- m=0: α_{-1}=0 and ker α_0=0, so C^0=0.
- m=1: B^0/α_0(A^0) ≅ Q_l^2/(diagonal Q_l) ≅ Q_l and ker α_1=0, so C^1 ≅ Q_l. Since F acts trivially on B^0 and α_0 is F-equivariant, F acts trivially on C^1.
- For 2≤m≤2d-1: if m=2i is even with 1≤i≤d-1, then α_m is an isomorphism so ker α_m=0, and m-1 is odd so B^{m-1}=0, hence the coker is 0; if m=2i+1 is odd with 1≤i≤d-1, then α_{m-1} is an isomorphism so the coker is 0, and A^m=0 so ker α_m=0. Thus C^m=0.
- m=2d: B^{2d-1}=0 and α_{2d}=0, so (1) gives C^{2d} ≅ ker α_{2d} = A^{2d}. This is an isomorphism of Q_l[F]-modules, and F acts on A^{2d} by q^d, so C^{2d} ≅ Q_l(-d).
- m=2d+1: B^{2d}=0 and A^{2d+1}=0, so C^{2d+1}=0.
- m>2d+1: all A and B vanish, so C^m=0.
The case d=1 is included: the range 2≤m≤2d-1 is empty, and H=P^0 was handled above.

Therefore H^*_{et,c}(U_k,Q_l) is concentrated in degrees 1 and 2d, with C^1 ≅ Q_l (trivial F) and C^{2d} ≅ Q_l(-d). Equivalently,
H^*_{et,c}(U_k,Q_l) ≅ Q_l[-1] ⊕ Q_l(-d)[-2d]. Both sides vanish outside degrees 1 and 2d; in degree 1 both are one-dimensional with trivial F-action, and in degree 2d both are one-dimensional with F acting by q^d. This proves the lemma.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be smooth projective geometrically connected varieties over \(\mathbb F_q\) of pure dimensions \(d_X\ge1\) and \(d_Y\ge1\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and use it to identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(\xi_X\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(\xi_Y\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle classes of \(\mathbb F_q\)-rational very ample divisors on \(X\) and on \(Y\), let \(L_X\) and \(L_Y\) be cup product with \(\xi_X\) and \(\xi_Y\), and suppose that \(L_X^{d_X-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d_X-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le n\le d_X\) and that \(L_Y^{d_Y-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d_Y-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le n\le d_Y\). Let \(\operatorname{pr}_1,\operatorname{pr}_2\) be the projections of \(X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y\), put \(\xi=\operatorname{pr}_1^*\xi_X+\operatorname{pr}_2^*\xi_Y\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), and let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\). Then \(L^{d_X+d_Y-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2(d_X+d_Y)-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X\times_{\mathbb F_q}Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every integer \(n\) with \(0\le n\le d_X+d_Y\).
proof: Proof. We invoke the proved lemma eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/d63243 with m=1, so that F_{q^m}=F_q and k is the algebraic closure of F_q as in the target statement. The hypotheses of the target supply smooth projective geometrically connected varieties X and Y of pure dimensions d_X,d_Y≥1 over F_q; F_q-rational very ample divisors H_X on X and H_Y on Y whose cycle classes are the given ξ_X and ξ_Y; the operators L_X and L_Y equal to cup product with ξ_X and ξ_Y; and the isomorphisms L_X^{d_X-n} and L_Y^{d_Y-n} for all 0≤n≤d_X and 0≤n≤d_Y respectively. These are exactly the hypotheses of eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/d63243 for m=1. In that lemma, ξ=pr_1^*ξ_X+pr_2^*ξ_Y is identified with the cycle class of the very ample divisor pr_1^*H_X+pr_2^*H_Y on X×_{F_q}Y, and L is cup product with ξ, again matching the target. Therefore eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/d63243 gives that L^{d_X+d_Y-n}: H^n_ét((X×_{F_q}Y)_k,Q_ℓ) → H^{2(d_X+d_Y)-n}_ét((X×_{F_q}Y)_k,Q_ℓ) is an isomorphism for every integer n with 0≤n≤d_X+d_Y. This is precisely the required assertion.

statement: Let k be a field of characteristic 0, let N ≥ 0 be an integer, and let H = ⊕_{n≥0} H^n be a finite-dimensional graded-commutative and graded-cocommutative Hopf algebra over k with H^0 = k. Suppose that dim_k H^1 = N, that H^n = 0 for every integer n > N, and that dim_k H^N = 1. Then for every integer n ≥ 0 the k-linear map ∧^n_k H^1 → H^n induced by the multiplication of H is an isomorphism.
proof:
Proof. Let Δ, ε, m, η denote the comultiplication, counit, multiplication and unit of H. For n ≥ 0 put P_n = {x ∈ H^n : Δ(x) = x⊗1 + 1⊗x}.

Step 1 (primitives of H). By eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/6e8b44, the primitive elements of H are exactly H^1. Since Δ is homogeneous of degree 0 and H is graded, an element x = Σ_n x_n is primitive if and only if each homogeneous component x_n is primitive. Hence P_1 = H^1 and P_n = 0 for every n ≥ 0 with n ≠ 1. In particular P_0 = 0 (equivalently, 1 is not primitive in characteristic 0, since Δ(1) = 1⊗1 ≠ 2·1⊗1).

Step 2 (the graded dual). Let B = H^* = ⊕_{n≥0} B^n with B^n = (H^n)^*. The evaluation pairing ⟨ , ⟩: B^n × H^n → k is perfect. Since H is finite-dimensional, B is a finite-dimensional graded Hopf algebra: its multiplication m_B: B^i ⊗ B^j → B^{i+j} is the transpose of Δ: H^{i+j} → H^i ⊗ H^j (with the usual Koszul sign convention), its unit is ε, its counit is evaluation at 1, and its comultiplication is the transpose of m. As H is graded-cocommutative, B is graded-commutative: for b ∈ B^i, c ∈ B^j and x ∈ H^{i+j}, the H^i⊗H^j-component of Δ(x) satisfies ⟨bc, x⟩ = (-1)^{ij}⟨b⊗c, Δ(x)⟩, while graded cocommutativity of H gives ⟨c⊗b, Δ(x)⟩ = (-1)^{ij}⟨b⊗c, Δ(x)⟩, whence ⟨bc, x⟩ = (-1)^{ij}⟨cb, x⟩ and therefore bc = (-1)^{ij}cb. Also B^0 = (H^0)^* = k, dim_k B^1 = N, B^n = 0 for n > N, and dim_k B^N = 1.

Step 3 (indecomposables of B versus primitives of H). Let B^+ = ⊕_{n≥1} B^n and Q(B) = B^+/(B^+)^2, graded by Q(B)_n = B^n/(B^+B^+)^n for n ≥ 1 and Q(B)_0 = 0, where (B^+B^+)^n = Σ_{i+j=n, i,j≥1} B^iB^j. We claim that for every n ≥ 1 the annihilator of (B^+B^+)^n in H^n = (B^n)^* is exactly P_n.

Indeed, fix x ∈ H^n. For i,j ≥ 1 with i+j = n, the bilinear form B^i × B^j → k, (b,c) ↦ ⟨bc, x⟩, is, up to the sign (-1)^{ij} which is invertible in k, the pairing of b⊗c with the H^i⊗H^j-component of Δ(x) under the perfect pairings B^i × H^i → k and B^j × H^j → k. Hence ⟨bc, x⟩ = 0 for all b ∈ B^i and c ∈ B^j if and only if the H^i⊗H^j-component of Δ(x) vanishes. Therefore x annihilates (B^+B^+)^n if and only if Δ(x) has no component in H^i⊗H^j for any i,j ≥ 1 with i+j = n, i.e. if and only if Δ(x) ∈ H^0⊗H^n ⊕ H^n⊗H^0.

Since H^0 = k·1, write Δ(x) = 1⊗x_1 + x_2⊗1 with x_1, x_2 ∈ H^n. Applying ε⊗id gives x = (ε⊗id)Δ(x) = x_1, because ε(x_2) = 0 as n ≥ 1. Applying id⊗ε gives x = x_2. Thus Δ(x) = 1⊗x + x⊗1, i.e. x ∈ P_n. Conversely, if x ∈ P_n, then for b ∈ B^i, c ∈ B^j with i,j ≥ 1 we have ⟨bc, x⟩ = (-1)^{ij}⟨b⊗c, Δ(x)⟩ = (-1)^{ij}(ε(b)⟨c,x⟩ + ⟨b,x⟩ε(c)) = 0, since ε vanishes on positive-degree elements. Hence the annihilator is P_n, and the perfect pairing identifies (Q(B)_n)^* with P_n; in particular dim_k Q(B)_n = dim_k P_n. By Step 1, Q(B)_1 ≅ (H^1)^* has dimension N, and Q(B)_n = 0 for all n ≥ 2.

Step 4 (B is generated by B^1). For n ≥ 2 the equality Q(B)_n = 0 means B^n = (B^+B^+)^n = Σ_{i=1}^{n-1} B^iB^{n-i}. We prove by induction on n that B^n is spanned by the n-fold products b_1···b_n with b_j ∈ B^1. For n = 0 this is B^0 = k (the empty product), and for n = 1 it is trivial. For n ≥ 2, by induction each B^i (1 ≤ i ≤ n-1) is spanned by i-fold products of elements of B^1 and each B^{n-i} is spanned by (n-i)-fold products; hence each B^iB^{n-i} is spanned by n-fold products, and their sum B^n is spanned by n-fold products. Thus B is generated as a graded k-algebra by B^1.

Step 5 (upper bound). Since B^1 lies in odd degree 1, graded commutativity of B gives b_1···b_i b_{i+1}···b_n = -b_1···b_{i+1}b_i···b_n for all b_1,...,b_n ∈ B^1. Hence the n-fold multiplication map (B^1)^{⊗n} → B^n is alternating and therefore factors through the canonical surjection (B^1)^{⊗n} → ∧^n B^1, producing a linear map ∧^n B^1 → B^n. By Step 4 this map is surjective. Consequently dim_k B^n ≤ dim_k ∧^n B^1 = binom(N,n), with the convention binom(N,n) = 0 for n > N.

Step 6 (lower bound). By Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_exterior_subalgebra_injects, the multiplication map ∧^n H^1 → H^n is injective for every n ≥ 0. Hence dim_k H^n ≥ dim_k ∧^n H^1 = binom(N,n).

Step 7 (conclusion). Since B^n = (H^n)^*, we have dim_k B^n = dim_k H^n. Combining Steps 5 and 6 gives binom(N,n) ≤ dim_k H^n = dim_k B^n ≤ binom(N,n), so dim_k H^n = binom(N,n). The injective linear map ∧^n H^1 → H^n therefore goes between finite-dimensional k-vector spaces of the same dimension, hence is an isomorphism. This holds for every n ≥ 0. (For N = 0 the same argument applies; explicitly H^1 = 0, H^n = 0 for n > 0, and the maps are the identity on k in degree 0 and zero maps between zero spaces in positive degrees.) ∎

statement: Let \(k\) be a field, let \(M\ge1\) be an integer, let \(C_1,\dots,C_M\) be smooth projective geometrically connected curves over \(k\), and let \(Z\subset C_1\times_k\cdots\times_k C_M\) be a closed subscheme of pure dimension \(n\) with \(0\le n\le M\). Then for every irreducible component \(W\) of \(Z\) there exist indices \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_n\le M\), the index set being empty when \(n=0\) and \(\operatorname{pr}_{i_1,\dots,i_n}\) then being the structure morphism to \(\operatorname{Spec}k\), such that the restriction of \(\operatorname{pr}_{i_1,\dots,i_n}\) to \(W\) is dominant onto its image and the induced extension of function fields is finite.
proof:
Proof. We prove the statement as written, with the indices allowed to depend on the irreducible component \(W\). If \(Z\) has no irreducible component, the assertion is vacuous. Assume \(Z\) is nonempty and put \(P=C_1\times_k\cdots\times_k C_M\). Fix an irreducible component \(W\) of \(Z\) and give it the reduced induced closed subscheme structure. Then \(W\) is integral and, since \(Z\) is pure of dimension \(n\), we have \(\dim W=n\).

We use the standard dimension theorem: if \(X\) is an integral scheme of finite type over a field \(k\), then \(\dim X=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(X)\). For completeness, here is a proof. Choose a nonempty affine open \(\operatorname{Spec} A\subset X\). Then \(A\) is a finitely generated \(k\)-domain with fraction field \(\kappa(X)\). By Noether normalization there exist algebraically independent elements \(y_1,\dots,y_d\in A\) over \(k\) such that \(A\) is finite as a module over \(k[y_1,\dots,y_d]\). Finite ring extensions preserve Krull dimension, so \(\dim A=d\), and \(d=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(X)\). Since \(X\) is integral, every nonempty open subscheme has the same dimension as \(X\), so \(\dim X=\dim A=d\).

For each \(i\), let \(x_i=\operatorname{pr}_i(\eta_W)\) be the image of the generic point of \(W\) in \(C_i\). Choose a nonempty affine open \(U_i\subset C_i\) containing \(x_i\), and put \(A_i=\mathcal O_{C_i}(U_i)\). Since \(C_i\) is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve, it is an integral scheme of finite type over \(k\) of dimension \(1\); hence \(A_i\) is a finitely generated \(k\)-domain of dimension \(1\). Let \(U=\prod_i U_i=\operatorname{Spec} A\), where \(A=A_1\otimes_k\cdots\otimes_k A_M\). Because \(\eta_W\) lies in \(U\), the open subscheme \(W\cap U\) is nonempty and dense in \(W\); it is integral and corresponds to a prime ideal \(\mathfrak p\subset A\). Put \(B=A/\mathfrak p\), so \(B\) is a domain with fraction field \(\kappa(W)\). For each \(i\), let \(B_i\) be the image of \(A_i\) in \(B\) and \(L_i=\operatorname{Frac}(B_i)\subset\kappa(W)\). Since \(B_i\) is a quotient of \(A_i\), it is a finitely generated \(k\)-domain of dimension at most \(1\); by the dimension theorem, \(\operatorname{trdeg}_k L_i=\dim B_i\le1\). The images of the \(A_i\) generate \(B\) as a \(k\)-algebra, hence the fields \(L_i\) generate \(\kappa(W)\) as a field over \(k\).

Since \(\kappa(W)\) is finitely generated over \(k\) and is generated by \(\bigcup_i L_i\), choose a finite subset \(T\subset\bigcup_i L_i\) which generates \(\kappa(W)\) as a field. Let \(S\) be a maximal algebraically independent subset of \(T\). Then \(S\) is a transcendence basis of \(\kappa(W)/k\): every \(t\in T\) is algebraic over \(k(S)\) by maximality, so \(\kappa(W)\) is algebraic over \(k(S)\). Therefore \(|S|=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(W)=\dim W=n\), by the dimension theorem and \(\dim W=n\). If \(S\) contained two distinct elements \(a,b\) of the same \(L_i\), then \(a,b\) would be algebraically independent over \(k\), so \(\operatorname{trdeg}_k L_i\ge2\), contradiction. Thus \(S\) contains at most one element from each \(L_i\). For each \(s\in S\), choose an index \(i(s)\) with \(s\in L_{i(s)}\). If \(s\ne t\) and \(i(s)=i(t)\), then both \(s\) and \(t\) lie in \(L_{i(s)}\), impossible; hence the indices \(i(s)\) are distinct. Sorting them gives \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_n\le M\) (the list is empty when \(n=0\)), and \(S\subset\bigcup_{j=1}^n L_{i_j}\).

Let \(P_I=\prod_{j=1}^n C_{i_j}\) (with \(P_I=\operatorname{Spec} k\) when \(n=0\)), and let \(\pi_I:P\to P_I\) be the projection. Let \(Y\subset P_I\) be the reduced closed subscheme whose underlying topological space is the closure of \(\pi_I(W)\). Then \(Y\) is integral and \(f=\pi_I|_W:W\to Y\) is dominant. We claim that \(\kappa(Y)\) is the compositum of the fields \(L_{i_j}\) inside \(\kappa(W)\). Indeed, over \(U_I=\prod_j U_{i_j}=\operatorname{Spec} A_I\) with \(A_I=\bigotimes_j A_{i_j}\), the morphism \(W\cap U\to U_I\) corresponds to the natural map \(A_I\to B\). Its scheme-theoretic image is \(\operatorname{Spec}(A_I/J)\), where \(J=\ker(A_I\to B)\), whose function field is the subfield of \(\kappa(W)\) generated by the images of the \(A_{i_j}\), i.e. the compositum of the \(L_{i_j}\). Passing to the closure in \(P_I\) does not change the function field, since \(Y\cap U_I\) is dense in \(Y\). Thus the claim holds. In particular, \(k(S)\subset\kappa(Y)\).

By the dimension theorem, \(\dim Y=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(Y)\). Since \(\kappa(Y)\subset\kappa(W)\), we have \(\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(Y)\le\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(W)=n\). Since \(k(S)\subset\kappa(Y)\) and \(|S|=n\), we have \(\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(Y)\ge n\). Hence \(\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(Y)=n\) and \(\dim Y=n\). We also have \(\dim W=n\), so \(f:W\to Y\) is a dominant morphism of integral varieties of the same dimension \(n\).

Apply lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_generic_fiber_integral to \(f:W\to Y\), taking its \(X\) to be our \(W\) and its integral closed subscheme to be the whole of \(X\). It says that the generic fibre \(W_\eta=W\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(Y)\) is integral of dimension \(\dim W-\dim Y=0\) and, since \(\dim W=\dim Y\), is the spectrum of a finite field extension of \(\kappa(Y)\) of degree \([\kappa(W):\kappa(Y)]\). Therefore \(\kappa(W)/\kappa(Y)\) is finite. Thus the restriction of \(\pi_I\) to \(W\) is dominant onto its image \(Y\) and induces a finite extension of function fields. Since \(W\) was an arbitrary irreducible component of \(Z\), the lemma follows.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let ⟨−,−⟩: V×V→K be a perfect bilinear form, and let T∈GL_K(V) satisfy ⟨Tx,Ty⟩=⟨x,y⟩ for all x,y∈V. Put N=T−id_V. If N^2=0 and rank N=1, then there exist a nonzero δ∈V and c∈K^× such that N(x)=c⟨x,δ⟩δ for all x∈V and ⟨δ,δ⟩=0.
proof:
Write the bilinear form as B(x,y)=⟨x,y⟩. Since N^2=0, we have T=id_V+N and (id_V+N)(id_V−N)=id_V−N^2=id_V, so T^{-1}=id_V−N. Both T and T^{-1} are isometries of the form.

For arbitrary x,y∈V, the isometry identity for T gives
0=⟨Tx,Ty⟩−⟨x,y⟩=⟨x+Nx,y+Ny⟩−⟨x,y⟩=⟨Nx,y⟩+⟨x,Ny⟩+⟨Nx,Ny⟩.  (1)
Similarly, the isometry identity for T^{-1} gives
0=⟨T^{-1}x,T^{-1}y⟩−⟨x,y⟩=⟨x−Nx,y−Ny⟩−⟨x,y⟩=−⟨Nx,y⟩−⟨x,Ny⟩+⟨Nx,Ny⟩.  (2)
Adding (1) and (2) yields 2⟨Nx,Ny⟩=0. Since char K=0, 2 is invertible, hence
⟨Nx,Ny⟩=0 for all x,y∈V.
Substituting this into (1) gives
⟨Nx,y⟩+⟨x,Ny⟩=0, i.e. ⟨Nx,y⟩=−⟨x,Ny⟩ for all x,y∈V.  (3)

Because rank N=1, the image of N is a one-dimensional subspace of V. Choose a nonzero vector δ spanning im N. Then there is a linear functional φ:V→K such that
N(x)=φ(x)δ for all x∈V.
Since N has rank 1, N≠0, so φ≠0. From N^2=0 we get, for every x∈V,
0=N^2(x)=N(φ(x)δ)=φ(x)N(δ)=φ(x)φ(δ)δ.
Choosing x with φ(x)≠0 and using δ≠0 gives φ(δ)=0. Thus N(δ)=φ(δ)δ=0.

Now put y=δ in (3). Since N(δ)=0, we obtain
0=⟨Nx,δ⟩=⟨φ(x)δ,δ⟩=φ(x)⟨δ,δ⟩
for every x∈V. Because φ≠0, choose x with φ(x)≠0; then ⟨δ,δ⟩=0.

Finally, using N(x)=φ(x)δ and N(y)=φ(y)δ in (3), we get
φ(x)⟨δ,y⟩=−φ(y)⟨x,δ⟩ for all x,y∈V.  (4)
Since the form is perfect and δ≠0, the linear functional y↦⟨δ,y⟩ is not identically zero; otherwise δ would lie in the radical of the form. Hence there exists y_0∈V with ⟨δ,y_0⟩≠0. Taking y=y_0 in (4) gives
φ(x)⟨δ,y_0⟩=−φ(y_0)⟨x,δ⟩,
so
φ(x)=c⟨x,δ⟩, where c=−φ(y_0)/⟨δ,y_0⟩.
If c were 0, then φ would be the zero functional, contradicting φ≠0. Therefore c∈K^×. Consequently,
N(x)=φ(x)δ=c⟨x,δ⟩δ for all x∈V,
and we have already shown ⟨δ,δ⟩=0. This proves the lemma.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ℓ≠p be a prime, and put k=F̄_q. Let S be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over F_q. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ℓ(1) and use it to identify Tate twists with Q_ℓ. Let H be an F_q-rational very ample divisor on S with cycle class ξ∈H²_ét(S_k,Q_ℓ), let L be cup product with ξ, put P²=ker(L:H²_ét(S_k,Q_ℓ)→H⁴_ét(S_k,Q_ℓ)), and let β(x,y)=tr_S(x∪y) for x,y∈H²_ét(S_k,Q_ℓ), where tr_S:H⁴_ét(S_k,Q_ℓ)→Q_ℓ is the Poincaré duality trace normalized by tr_S(cl(z))=[κ(z):F_q] for closed points z of S. Let W be the Q-linear span of the cycle classes of the F_q-rational divisors D on S with cl(D)∈P², and suppose that P²=W⊗_Q Q_ℓ. Then for every field embedding σ:Q̄_ℓ↪C, the Hermitian form h_σ on W⊗_{Q,σ}C defined by h_σ(x⊗a,y⊗b)=a·conj(b)·β(x,y) is negative definite.
proof:
Let \(H^2=H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(H^4=H^4_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(S_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Since \(S\) is smooth projective over \(k\) and \(\ell\neq p\), these are finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces, and \(\operatorname{tr}_S\colon H^4\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) is the Poincaré duality trace normalized as in the statement.

**Step 0 (bilinearity and symmetry of \(\beta\)).** The cup product is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-bilinear and \(\operatorname{tr}_S\) is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear, hence \(\beta\) is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-bilinear. For \(x,y\in H^2\), graded commutativity of the cup product gives \(x\cup y=(-1)^{2\cdot 2}y\cup x=y\cup x\), so \(\beta(x,y)=\beta(y,x)\). Thus \(\beta\) is a symmetric \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-bilinear form on \(H^2\).

**Step 1 (\(W\subseteq P^2\) and its generators).** The map \(L\colon H^2\to H^4\), \(x\mapsto x\cup\xi\), is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear, so \(P^2=\ker L\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-subspace of \(H^2\). By definition \(W\) is the \(\mathbb Q\)-linear span of the classes \(\operatorname{cl}(D)\in P^2\) of \(F_q\)-rational divisors \(D\); since \(P^2\) is closed under addition and under multiplication by \(\mathbb Q\subseteq\mathbb Q_\ell\), we have \(W\subseteq P^2\). Every element \(x\in W\) is, by definition, a finite \(\mathbb Q\)-linear combination \(x=\sum_i q_i\operatorname{cl}(D_i)\) with \(q_i\in\mathbb Q\) and \(D_i\) \(F_q\)-rational divisors such that \(\operatorname{cl}(D_i)\in P^2\). Since \(S\) is smooth, each divisor \(D_i\) is a Cartier divisor.

**Step 2 (negative values and rationality on \(W\)).** Let \(x\in W\setminus\{0\}\). Then \(x\in P^2\) by Step 1, and \(x\) is a nonzero \(\mathbb Q\)-linear combination of cycle classes of \(F_q\)-rational Cartier divisors. Applying Miner/16d24b0281973336/d3e72a with \(m=1\) (so \(F_{q^m}=F_q\)) to the surface \(S\), the very ample divisor \(H\), the class \(\xi\), the map \(L\), the space \(P^2\), the trace \(\operatorname{tr}_S\), and the form \(\beta\), we obtain
\[
\beta(x,x)\in\mathbb Q_{<0}. \tag{2.1}
\]
Now let \(x,y\in W\). If \(x+y\neq0\), then by (2.1) \(\beta(x+y,x+y)\in\mathbb Q\), and also \(\beta(x,x)\in\mathbb Q\) and \(\beta(y,y)\in\mathbb Q\) (with the convention \(\beta(0,0)=0\)). Hence
\[
2\beta(x,y)=\beta(x+y,x+y)-\beta(x,x)-\beta(y,y)\in\mathbb Q,
\]
so \(\beta(x,y)\in\mathbb Q\). If \(x+y=0\), then \(\beta(x,y)=-\beta(x,x)\in\mathbb Q\). Therefore
\[
\beta(W,W)\subseteq\mathbb Q. \tag{2.2}
\]

**Step 3 (well-definedness and Hermitian symmetry of \(h_\sigma\)).** Let \(\sigma\colon\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\) be a field embedding. Since \(\operatorname{char}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell=0\), the restriction \(\sigma|_{\mathbb Q}\colon\mathbb Q\to\mathbb C\) is a field homomorphism, hence \(\sigma(q)=q\) for every \(q\in\mathbb Q\). By (2.2), \(\sigma(\beta(x,y))=\beta(x,y)\) for all \(x,y\in W\). Also, since \(\sigma|_{\mathbb Q}=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb Q}\), the tensor product \(W\otimes_{\mathbb Q,\sigma}\mathbb C\) is the ordinary tensor product \(W\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C\).

Define \(h_\sigma\) on elementary tensors by
\[
h_\sigma(x\otimes a,y\otimes b)=a\,\overline{b}\,\beta(x,y),\qquad x,y\in W,\ a,b\in\mathbb C.
\]
We check that this is well defined on the balanced tensor product. For \(\lambda\in\mathbb Q\), in the first variable \((\lambda x)\otimes a=x\otimes(\sigma(\lambda)a)=x\otimes(\lambda a)\), and
\[
h_\sigma(\lambda x\otimes a,y\otimes b)=a\overline{b}\beta(\lambda x,y)=\lambda a\overline{b}\beta(x,y)=h_\sigma(x\otimes\lambda a,y\otimes b).
\]
In the second variable \((\lambda y)\otimes b=y\otimes(\lambda b)\), and
\[
h_\sigma(x\otimes a,\lambda y\otimes b)=a\overline{b}\beta(x,\lambda y)=\lambda a\overline{b}\beta(x,y)=a\overline{\lambda b}\beta(x,y)=h_\sigma(x\otimes a,y\otimes\lambda b),
\]
where we used \(\overline{\lambda}=\lambda\) for \(\lambda\in\mathbb Q\subseteq\mathbb R\). Additivity in each variable follows from the bilinearity of \(\beta\). Hence \(h_\sigma\) is well defined. It is \(\mathbb C\)-linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second, and
\[
h_\sigma(y\otimes b,x\otimes a)=b\overline{a}\beta(y,x)=\overline{a\overline{b}\beta(x,y)}=\overline{h_\sigma(x\otimes a,y\otimes b)},
\]
because \(\beta(y,x)=\beta(x,y)\in\mathbb Q\subseteq\mathbb R\). Thus \(h_\sigma\) is a Hermitian form on \(W\otimes_{\mathbb Q,\sigma}\mathbb C\).

**Step 4 (negative definiteness of \(h_\sigma\)).** If \(W=0\), the assertion is vacuous. Assume \(W\neq0\). By the hypothesis \(P^2=W\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb Q_\ell\) and the flatness of \(\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q_\ell\), the natural map \(W\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb Q_\ell\to H^2\) is injective with image \(P^2\), so \(\dim_{\mathbb Q}W=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}P^2<\infty\). Put \(m=\dim_{\mathbb Q}W\ge1\) and choose a \(\mathbb Q\)-basis \(x_1,\dots,x_m\) of \(W\). Let
\[
B=(\beta(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^m\in M_m(\mathbb Q),
\]
which is symmetric by Step 0 and rational by (2.2).

For every \(c=(c_1,\dots,c_m)^T\in\mathbb Q^m\setminus\{0\}\), the element \(\sum_i c_i x_i\in W\) is nonzero because \(x_1,\dots,x_m\) is a basis, so by (2.1)
\[
c^TBc=\beta\Big(\sum_i c_i x_i,\sum_j c_j x_j\Big)<0. \tag{4.1}
\]
In particular \(B\) is negative definite over \(\mathbb Q\), hence nondegenerate: if \(Bc=0\) with \(c\in\mathbb Q^m\), then \(c^TBc=0\), so \(c=0\) by (4.1).

We now diagonalize \(B\) by symmetric Gram–Schmidt over \(\mathbb Q\). We construct a \(\mathbb Q\)-basis \(v_1,\dots,v_m\) of \(\mathbb Q^m\) with
\[
v_i^TBv_j=0\quad(i\neq j),\qquad v_i^TBv_i=-d_i,\quad d_i\in\mathbb Q_{>0}.
\]
Inductively, suppose \(v_1,\dots,v_k\) (\(k<m\)) have been constructed with the stated orthogonality. Let
\[
U_k=\{c\in\mathbb Q^m: v_i^TBc=0\text{ for }i=1,\dots,k\}.
\]
Each functional \(c\mapsto v_i^TBc\) is nonzero because \(B\) is nondegenerate and \(v_i\neq0\); hence \(U_k\) is the intersection of \(k\) proper hyperplanes in \(\mathbb Q^m\), so \(\dim_{\mathbb Q}U_k\ge m-k>0\). Choose \(v_{k+1}\in U_k\setminus\{0\}\). Then \(v_{k+1}^TBv_{k+1}<0\) by (4.1), so \(d_{k+1}:=-v_{k+1}^TBv_{k+1}\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\). Moreover \(v_{k+1}\notin\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}(v_1,\dots,v_k)\): otherwise \(v_{k+1}=\sum_{i\le k}a_iv_i\) and then \(v_{k+1}^TBv_{k+1}=\sum_i a_i(v_i^TBv_{k+1})=0\), a contradiction. Thus \(v_1,\dots,v_{k+1}\) are \(\mathbb Q\)-linearly independent. After \(m\) steps we obtain a \(\mathbb Q\)-basis.

Let \(P\in GL_m(\mathbb Q)\) be the matrix whose columns are \(v_1,\dots,v_m\). Then
\[
P^TBP=D:=\operatorname{diag}(-d_1,\dots,-d_m),\qquad d_i\in\mathbb Q_{>0},
\]
equivalently
\[
B=P^{-T}DP^{-1}. \tag{4.2}
\]

Now let \(v=\sum_{i=1}^m x_i\otimes a_i\in W\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C\) be nonzero, with \(a_i\in\mathbb C\). Since \(x_1,\dots,x_m\) is a \(\mathbb Q\)-basis of \(W\), the elements \(x_i\otimes1\) form a \(\mathbb C\)-basis of \(W\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C\); hence \(a=(a_1,\dots,a_m)^T\neq0\). Using (4.2) and the symmetry of \(B\),
\[
h_\sigma(v,v)=\sum_{i,j}a_i\overline{a_j}\beta(x_i,x_j)=a^*Ba=a^*P^{-T}DP^{-1}a.
\]
Put \(b=P^{-1}a\in\mathbb C^m\); then \(b\neq0\) because \(P\) is invertible and \(a\neq0\), and
\[
h_\sigma(v,v)=b^*Db=-\sum_{i=1}^m d_i|b_i|^2<0,
\]
because every \(d_i\) is a positive real number and \(b\neq0\). Hence \(h_\sigma\) is negative definite.

**Remark on the corrected linear algebra.** The previous attempt claimed that from (4.1) one can find \(P\in GL_m(\mathbb Q)\) with \(P^TBP=-I_m\), equivalently \(B=-N^TN\) with \(N\in GL_m(\mathbb Q)\). This is false: for example \(B=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\1&-9\end{pmatrix}\) is negative definite over \(\mathbb Q\) (its leading principal minors are \(-2<0\) and \(\det B=17>0\)), but \(\det B=17\) is not a square in \(\mathbb Q\), whereas \(\det(-N^TN)=\det(N)^2\) would be. The correct conclusion of symmetric Gram–Schmidt over \(\mathbb Q\) is \(P^TBP=\operatorname{diag}(-d_1,\dots,-d_m)\) with \(d_i\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\), which is exactly what is proved above and is sufficient, since the \(d_i\) are positive real numbers and hence \(-\sum_i d_i|b_i|^2<0\) for \(b\neq0\). No rational factorization \(B=-N^TN\) is needed or asserted.

This completes the proof.
